text: William Valentine Schevill studied with Frank Duveneck at the Cincinnati Art Academy and then at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich with Ludwig Löfftz, Max Lindenschmitt and Nikolaos Gyzis. He lived in Los Angeles in the 1940s and was active in New York City and Boston. He was a member of the Salmagundi Club. He showed at the Louisiana Purchase Exposition. His work is at the Herron School of Art and Design and the National Portrait Gallery. He was born in Cincinnati in 1864 and died in 1951.

Francesco Torbido, also called il Moro, studied under Giorgione in Venice and then went to Verona, where he married the daughter of Count Zenovello Giusti. In the Count's service he became a pupil of Liberale da Verona, who adopted him as his heir. In Venice he painted frescoes of the Life of the Virgin and a Transfiguration. In 1534 he painted lunettes of the Nativity and an Assumption of the Virgin for the main chapel of Verona cathedral. He also painted several portraits, among them two self-portraits, and worked for the Basilica di San Zeno.

Frans Francken III is the best known member of the fourth generation of the Francken family of artists. He was the son of Frans Francken II and became a master in the Antwerp Guild of St. Luke in 1639. He was dean of the guild for ten years from 1656. He painted genre works and portraits, and he added figures to the works of Pieter Neeffs I. His figures follow his father's style but are painted with less accuracy, and his strong debt to Rubens earned him the nickname the Rubensian Francken.

James Roberts painted a portrait of James Smithson in Oxford in 1786, when Smithson graduated with an M.A. He showed work at the Royal Academy every year. For John Bell's book series Bell's British Theatre he made over 60 watercolours on vellum of actors in dramatic roles. In Oxford he worked as a drawing master and fell under the influence of John Baptist Malchair. His portrait of John Hawkins was the only one for which Hawkins sat. He painted scenery at Blenheim Palace too.

Leopold von der Decken changed his name to John Decker when he emigrated from Berlin to America in 1921. In World War I he was interned on the Isle of Man as an enemy alien. He worked as a cartoonist for the New York Evening World until 1928, when he moved to Hollywood and took up fine art. Film stars such as Errol Flynn, Charlie Chaplin and Greta Garbo commissioned portraits from him. The paintings of the frustrated artist in Fritz Lang's film Scarlet Street were his.

John Kelt Edwards took the middle name Kelt on the advice of Augusta, the daughter of Baroness Llanover, who said a common name like John Edwards was unlikely to stand out. He came from Blaenau Ffestiniog and studied engraving in Wolverhampton. He later studied under Léon Bonnat at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and exhibited at the Paris Salon. In 1902 he painted 12 pictures for Daniel Rees's Welsh translation of Dante's Divine Comedy, his first important Welsh commission. He also made illustrations for Welsh books and magazines.

Nicolas Jean Baptiste Poilly worked as a draftsman and engraver in France and lived from 1707 to 1780. The Cooper-Hewitt, National Design Museum holds his work, and so does the National Portrait Gallery in London. A print he made in 1746 follows a portrait by Domenico Duprà. His subjects also include King Porus before Alexander and a view of St Paul's Cathedral.

John Syme studied at the Trustees' Academy on Picardy Place in Edinburgh and became a pupil and assistant of Sir Henry Raeburn. He completed Raeburn's unfinished works. He then worked as a successful portrait painter in Edinburgh. Syme was an original member of the Royal Scottish Academy, founded in 1826, and took an active part in managing it. He was a nephew of Patrick Syme. William Home Lizars commissioned a portrait from him.

Adam Gorczyński wrote popular novels in the style of the noble gawęda under the pseudonym Jadam of Zator, and he also painted Polish landscapes. He was born in Tarnów in 1805, the son of an ennobled lawyer, and he studied philosophy in Lviv. From 1821 he took chamber studies in Vienna, which prepared estate managers for large landownership. He was a co-founder of the Kraków Society of Friends of Fine Arts and owner of estates in Brzeźnica and Marcyporęba. Today he is the patron of cultural initiatives in his hometown of Brzeźnica.

Leib Sonder, later known as Aleksander Sochaczewski, came from a Jewish family. He entered the Warsaw Academy. In 1862 he was arrested after a search of his apartment turned up equipment for making bullets and underground publications. He was sentenced to death in 1863, but the sentence was changed to hard labor in Siberia. His prison term ended in 1883, and he emigrated to Munich, then lived in Brussels and settled in Vienna. Siberia left a mark.

Angiolo Tommasi belonged to the Macchiaioli movement. His brother Ludovico and his cousin Adolfo were painters too, and all three were influential in Tuscany. He first studied at the Scuola Comunale di Disegno in Livorno and then spent two years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Florence. Silvestro Lega then mentored him in painting landscapes, as he did his family members. At the Promotrice of Florence in 1882 he showed small views. A painting from 1885 shows peasants kneeling outside a small church at the moment of the elevation of the host.

Antoine-Marie Chenavard worked as an architect, a professor and a road inspector in France. He traveled to Greece and the Levant in 1843 and 1844 and published an account of the trip. He also published a collection of 12 original drawings of the monuments of Athens in 1841. His other books collect sketches of fountains and of subjects drawn from the poems of Ossian. He also wrote about ancient Lyon.

Attilio Simonetti was the son of a Roman jeweler and engraver, and his mother came from a family of mosaicists. His talent was noticed early by a family friend, the painter Marià Fortuny. He began formal studies at sixteen. In 1877 he showed copies of two paintings at the national exhibition in Naples, and the future King Umberto I bought them. In 1875 he was among the founders of an association of watercolorists. After Fortuny died, Simonetti acted as executor for the sale of the antiquities Fortuny had collected, and that led him to open his own antiques business.

Auguste Clot printed lithographs for artists such as Pierre Bonnard, Maurice Denis, Paul Cézanne, Auguste Rodin, Marie Duhem and Edvard Munch. He began his career working for Lemercier in Paris and founded his own atelier in the mid-1890s. He often worked with the art dealer and publisher Ambroise Vollard. He was born in Paris in 1858 and died in Villeneuve-Saint-Georges in 1936.

Belbello da Pavia caught the attention of Duke Filippo Maria Visconti in Milan, soon after leaving his birthplace Pavia. The Duke assigned him to continue the Book of Hours of Gian Galeazzo Visconti, and the illustrations show his changing style. Later he moved to Mantua and began painting a Missal for Gianlucido Gonzaga in 1448. He had to leave Mantua in 1450 because of a moral misdemeanor. In 1461 the Marchioness of Mantua gave the Missal to Girolamo da Cremona, and the next year he moved to Venice.

Carl Gaertner spent his whole life in Cleveland. He studied at the Cleveland School of Art, now the Cleveland Institute of Art, and taught there from 1925 until he died. Early in his career he painted industrial subjects with Cleveland as his model. After 1935 he bought a farm in the Chagrin Valley and began a series of paintings of that subject. The Akron Art Museum holds three paintings by him, among them Riverside Plant and Summer Kitchen.

Edward Tennyson Reed was the son of Sir Edward James Reed, the Chief Naval Architect and MP for Cardiff. He went to Harrow and studied for the Bar but preferred art. After little success as a portrait painter, he turned to caricature and began drawing for Punch in 1889. In 1893 he succeeded Harry Furniss as the political caricaturist of Punch, and his satirical portraits illustrated the Essence of Parliament articles for eighteen years. His series Prehistoric Peeps became a silent film in 1905. He stayed with Punch until his death.

Fabrizio Galliari came from a large family of artists and followed his brother Bernardino to Milan to study stage design. Their careers overlapped so closely that their work is hard to tell apart, though Fabrizio concentrated on architecture. Together they decorated the Visconti castle at Brignano Gera d'Adda with trompe l'oeil architecture and landscape. In 1738 Fabrizio painted a triumphal arch for the arrival in Venice of Maria Amalia of Saxony, who was on her way to be married. He also painted the trompe-l'oeil dome of Vercelli Cathedral.

Francesco Bonsignori studied with Liberale da Verona, and his early style shows that influence. In 1487 he became portraitist and court artist to the Gonzaga family of Mantua, where Andrea Mantegna also worked. The two collaborated on several paintings of the Madonna and Child, and the attribution of some works is debated because their techniques are so alike. For about eleven years no official record of his activity survives. His late style was decisively influenced by Lorenzo Costa. He made his last monumental altarpiece in 1519, shortly before he died.

Francesco Panini was one of two sons of the famous veduta painter Giovanni Paolo Panini. His brother Giuseppe was an architect and archaeologist who completed the Trevi Fountain, and the two worked together at different stages of their careers. Around 1770 Francesco created a series of hand-coloured views of St. Peter's Basilica. He then worked with the engraver Giovanni Volpato, who published a large series of plates after the frescoes of the Raphael Rooms and the loggias at the Vatican. He also collaborated with other engravers in Rome and published prints.

François Dumoulin was meant for a commercial career, but in 1776 he became a witness to the American War of Independence and drew several naval battles between the French and British navies. Back in Vevey he turned his sketches into oil paintings and watercolours and earned his living by giving drawing lessons. Two of his paintings of naval battles were shown at the 1796 Salon in Paris. In 1810 he published 150 engravings on the journey of Robinson Crusoe, which is considered a precursor to modern comics.

Frantz Charlet, an Impressionist, was one of the founding members of the group Les XX. He worked as a painter, etcher and lithographer in Belgium. He studied at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels, first in the early 1870s and again from 1876, under Jean-François Portaels. His fellow pupils there included Théo van Rysselberghe and Rodolphe Wytsman. He lived from 1862 to 1928.

Georgy Pashkov designed the first postage stamps of the Soviet Union in 1923. He came from a Moscow family of iconographers that had the patronage of the Imperial family. With his brothers Pavel and Nikolai he graduated from the Stroganov Art School. In 1912 he and Nikolai decorated the lower church of the Feodorovsky Imperial Cathedral in Tsarskoye Selo, and the brothers received the title of Court Artists. He also created a large number of advertising posters before World War I.

Giovanni Giacomo Barbelli painted religious and mythological scenes on canvas and in fresco for churches and residences in Lombardy. He was born in Offanengo near Crema and learned drawing and painting in Naples while young. He painted the vaults and walls of grand rooms with an inventive imagination and a good knowledge of perspective. He is mentioned as a mentor of Evaristo Baschenis. His works include a Nativity altarpiece for the sanctuary of Nostra Signora della Brughiera in Bulliana. He was also a highly skilled draughtsman.

Gianfrancesco Penni, called il Fattore, came from a family of weavers in Florence and entered Raphael's workshop very early. He worked with Raphael on the Rooms of the Vatican Palace and the frescoes of the Villa Farnesina in Rome. After Raphael's early death he worked with Giulio Romano to complete the Hall of Constantine, the Transfiguration and the Palazzo Te in Mantua. His brothers were artists too, Bartolommeo at the court of Henry VIII and Luca at Fontainebleau. He also designed tapestries of the life of Christ for Clement VII.

Henry Bataille lost his parents when he was young. He attended the École des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Julian to study painting, but he had started writing at fourteen. His second play, La Lépreuse of 1896, was a success, and after it he became a playwright exclusively. His early works explored the effects of passion on human motivation and how stifling social conventions were. Later he moved toward the theatre of ideas and social drama. He also made prints.

Ivan Vishnyakov was briefly apprenticed to a varnisher before he was sent to the Chancellory of Buildings in 1727. There he studied under the French portrait painter Louis Caravaque and Andrey Matveyev. In 1739 he qualified as a master painter, and after Matveyev's early death he became head of the Chancellory. He painted murals in many palaces and churches of Saint Petersburg, among them the Summer Palace, the Anichkov Palace and the Winter Palace. His portraits were among the first to depart from the flat, static style favored at the Imperial Court.

James Sowerby decided to become a painter of flowers, and his first venture was illustrating William Curtis's Flora Londinensis. He studied art at the Royal Academy and took an apprenticeship with Richard Wright. The botanist L'Héritier de Brutelle invited him to provide the plates for his monograph Geranologia, an early commission that led to his prominence. He also made the plates for English Botany, using vivid colour and accessible texts to reach a widening audience. He and his wife Anne had seven children, and three of his sons became naturalists too.

Jean-Jacques Boissard left the seminary at Leuven in secret and traveled to Italy, where he was often poor. His time there gave him a taste for antiquities, and he collected artefacts from Rome and its surroundings. He later withdrew to Metz because he could not publicly profess the Protestant religion. He provided text and drawings for books by Theodor de Bry and Jacques Granthomme, among others. His Habitus Variarum Orbis Gentium of 1581 is ornamented with seventy illuminated figures. He also wrote Latin poetry.

John Baptist Medina was the first illustrator of Milton's Paradise Lost, in 1688. He was born in Brussels, the son of a Spanish army captain, and trained there under François Duchatel. He came to London in 1686 and later moved to Edinburgh at the invitation of the Earl of Leven. There he became the most prominent Scottish portraitist, charging 5 pounds for a head and 10 pounds for a half-length. His best known works are about 30 oval bust-lengths in Surgeons' Hall in Edinburgh, which are often compared to Godfrey Kneller's Kit-Cat Club series in London.

John Henry Bufford trained in the Pendleton lithography shop in Boston and moved to New York in 1835, where he worked independently for five years while accepting commissions from George Endicott and Nathaniel Currier. In 1839 he returned to Boston and became chief artist in the print shop of Benjamin Thayer. The shop later took his name. His firm made sheet music, city views, book illustrations, factory scenes and portraits copied from daguerreotypes. Winslow Homer and Leopold Grozelier were among the artists who worked for him.
